chapters.title: Empire and the Great War
chapters.text:
To understand twentieth-century Germany, we have to start a little earlier, in 1871. In that year, after a short and victorious war against France, the many German states were united into a single empire, proclaimed in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles. Its emperor, the Kaiser, was the King of Prussia, and its capital was Berlin. The architect of unification was the Prussian chancellor, Otto von Bismarck.

The new Germany grew at astonishing speed. Within a generation it became an industrial giant, with coal and steel in the Ruhr, a world-leading chemical and electrical industry, and the best universities in Europe. Berlin's population exploded, from under a million to around two million people, with grand boulevards, department stores, and crowded tenement blocks for the workers. Germany had a parliament, the Reichstag, elected by all adult men, and the largest socialist party in Europe. But real power rested with the Kaiser, his ministers and the army, and the officer corps, dominated by Prussian aristocrats, enjoyed enormous prestige.

In 1888, the young Wilhelm the Second became Kaiser. He dismissed Bismarck and pursued a more aggressive policy, demanding for Germany a place in the sun: colonies, and a navy to rival Britain's. Europe divided into two armed camps. Germany and Austria-Hungary on one side; France, Russia and, increasingly, Britain on the other.

In June 1914, the heir to the Austrian throne was assassinated in Sarajevo. Germany gave Austria-Hungary unconditional support, the so-called blank cheque, and within weeks a regional crisis became a continental war. Germany's war plan, drawn up by General von Schlieffen, called for a rapid knockout blow against France through neutral Belgium, before turning east against Russia. The invasion of Belgium brought Britain into the war.

In August 1914, crowds in Berlin cheered the troops, and many believed the war would be over by Christmas. Instead, the German advance was stopped at the river Marne, near Paris, and the Western Front froze into a line of trenches from the Channel to Switzerland. For four years, millions of men fought over a few kilometres of mud, at places like Verdun and the Somme. In the east, the war was more mobile, and Germany won great victories over Russia.

At home, the British naval blockade caused severe shortages. The winter of 1916 to 1917 became known as the turnip winter, when hundreds of thousands of civilians died of hunger and disease. The army's supreme command, under Generals Hindenburg and Ludendorff, effectively ran the country. In 1917, the United States entered the war, and Russia collapsed into revolution. Germany imposed a harsh peace on the new Bolshevik regime and, in the spring of 1918, threw everything into a final offensive in the west. It failed.

By the autumn of 1918, the German army was exhausted and retreating, and its allies were falling away. Ludendorff himself demanded an armistice, but he made sure that civilian politicians would be the ones to ask for it. At the beginning of November, sailors at Kiel mutinied rather than sail out for a last suicidal battle. The revolt spread across the country. On the ninth of November, in Berlin, the Kaiser's abdication was announced, and a republic was proclaimed from the Reichstag. Wilhelm fled to exile in the Netherlands. Two days later, on the eleventh of November, the armistice was signed.

About two million German soldiers had died. And because the war ended while German troops still stood on foreign soil, many Germans refused to believe they had really been defeated. Instead, a poisonous legend spread: that the army had been stabbed in the back by socialists, Jews and politicians at home. This lie would haunt the new republic from its very first day.

chapters.title: The Weimar Republic
chapters.text:
The republic born in November 1918 took its name from the small town of Weimar, where its constitution was written, far from the violence of Berlin. On paper it was one of the most democratic states in the world. Women could vote for the first time, and a system of proportional representation gave a voice to every political current. But the republic faced enemies on both sides from the very start.

In January 1919, communists tried to seize power in Berlin. The Social Democratic government turned to the army and to the Freikorps, volunteer units of former soldiers, to crush the uprising. The communist leaders Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht were captured and murdered. The left never forgave the Social Democrats. Meanwhile, the right never forgave the republic for accepting defeat.

In June 1919, Germany signed the Treaty of Versailles. It lost territory, including Alsace-Lorraine and land to the new Polish state, all its colonies, and most of its army. It accepted responsibility for the war and was required to pay reparations. Almost every German, from left to right, considered the treaty a humiliation. Nationalists called the politicians who had signed it the November criminals. In 1920, right-wing soldiers attempted a coup in Berlin, the Kapp Putsch, which collapsed after a general strike. Political murders became common: the foreign minister, Walther Rathenau, a Jew, was shot dead in 1922.

Then came 1923, the year of chaos. When Germany fell behind on reparations, French and Belgian troops occupied the Ruhr, the industrial heart of the country. The government responded by printing money, and inflation spiralled out of control. By November, a loaf of bread cost two hundred billion marks. People carried wages in wheelbarrows, and the savings of the middle class were wiped out. In Munich, an obscure agitator named Adolf Hitler tried to launch a national revolution from a beer hall. The putsch failed, Hitler went to prison, and there he wrote Mein Kampf.

And then, surprisingly, things got better. A new currency stopped the inflation. American loans flowed in, and reparations were rescheduled. Under foreign minister Gustav Stresemann, Germany made peace with France and joined the League of Nations. These were the Golden Twenties. Berlin became the most exciting city in Europe: the city of cabaret and jazz, of the Bauhaus and expressionist cinema, of Bertolt Brecht, Marlene Dietrich and Albert Einstein. It was also a city of open homosexual life and of sharp social contrasts.

The stability was fragile. In October 1929, Stresemann died, and weeks later the Wall Street crash ended the flow of American money. Germany was hit harder than almost any other country. By 1932, six million Germans were unemployed. The parliamentary system broke down: parties could not agree on a majority, and from 1930 chancellors governed by emergency decree, signed by the president, the old war hero Paul von Hindenburg.

The crisis was Hitler's opportunity. His National Socialist German Workers' Party, the Nazis, promised work, national rebirth, and revenge on the enemies supposedly responsible for Germany's misery: the Versailles powers, the Marxists, and above all, the Jews. Its brown-shirted stormtroopers, the SA, fought communists in the streets. In 1928 the Nazis won less than three percent of the vote. In July 1932, they won thirty-seven percent and became the largest party in the Reichstag. The communists also grew. The democratic centre was collapsing.

Hitler never won a majority in a free election. He came to power through a deal. A small group of conservative politicians around Hindenburg, led by the former chancellor Franz von Papen, believed they could use Hitler's mass movement and keep him under control. On the thirtieth of January 1933, Hindenburg appointed Hitler Chancellor of Germany, in a cabinet where Nazis were a minority. That night, the SA marched with torches through the Brandenburg Gate. Papen boasted that within two months they would have pushed Hitler into a corner. He could not have been more wrong.

chapters.title: The Nazi Dictatorship
chapters.text:
It took Hitler barely eighteen months to destroy German democracy. On the twenty-seventh of February 1933, the Reichstag building burned. A young Dutch communist was arrested at the scene, and the Nazis claimed it was the signal for a communist uprising. The next day, Hindenburg signed an emergency decree suspending freedom of speech, of the press and of assembly. Thousands of communists and social democrats were arrested, beaten and held in improvised camps, often in cellars run by the SA. One of the first permanent concentration camps opened at Dachau, near Munich, in March.

In new elections, held in an atmosphere of terror, the Nazis still won only forty-four percent. But on the twenty-third of March, the Reichstag passed the Enabling Act, which allowed Hitler's government to make laws without parliament. Only the Social Democrats voted against it; the communist deputies had already been arrested or had fled. Within months, every other party was banned or dissolved itself. Trade unions were abolished. The states lost their independence. The process was called Gleichschaltung, the coordination of all German life under the Nazi Party.

Culture was purged. In May 1933, students burned books by Jewish, socialist and pacifist authors in Berlin and in university towns across the country. Artists, scientists and writers emigrated in their thousands, Albert Einstein and Thomas Mann among them. Joseph Goebbels, minister of propaganda, took control of the press, radio and film.

In June 1934, Hitler turned on his own movement. The SA, led by Ernst Röhm, had grown to millions of men and was demanding a second revolution, alarming the army. In the Night of the Long Knives, the SS murdered Röhm and dozens of other SA leaders, as well as conservative opponents. The army was grateful. When Hindenburg died in August, Hitler merged the offices of president and chancellor and became the Führer. Every soldier swore an oath of personal loyalty to him.

For many Germans, the following years felt like a recovery. Unemployment fell rapidly, thanks to public works like the motorways and, above all, to massive and secret rearmament. In 1935, Hitler announced conscription, openly breaking the Treaty of Versailles. In 1936, German troops reoccupied the demilitarised Rhineland, and Britain and France did nothing. That summer, Berlin hosted the Olympic Games, a carefully staged showcase of the new Germany.

Behind the façade, the police state grew. The Gestapo, the secret police, and the SS under Heinrich Himmler built a system of surveillance and terror that relied heavily on denunciations by ordinary citizens. And from the very beginning, the regime persecuted Germany's Jews, around half a million people, less than one percent of the population. In April 1933, there was a boycott of Jewish shops, and Jews were removed from the civil service. In 1935, the Nuremberg Laws stripped Jews of citizenship and banned marriage between Jews and other Germans. Step by step, Jews were pushed out of professions, schools and public life.

On the night of the ninth of November 1938, the regime unleashed a nationwide pogrom, later called Kristallnacht, the night of broken glass. Synagogues were burned, thousands of Jewish shops were destroyed, around a hundred people were killed, and some thirty thousand Jewish men were sent to concentration camps. Many Jews now tried desperately to leave, but most countries refused to take more than a few refugees.

Abroad, Hitler moved from success to success. In March 1938, German troops marched into Austria, which was annexed to the Reich amid cheering crowds. In September, at the Munich conference, Britain and France agreed to let Germany take the Sudetenland, the German-speaking border areas of Czechoslovakia, in the hope of preserving peace. Six months later, Hitler occupied the rest of the Czech lands. Britain and France finally guaranteed Poland's independence. In August 1939, Germany shocked the world by signing a non-aggression pact with its ideological enemy, the Soviet Union, with a secret protocol dividing Eastern Europe between them. Hitler now had a free hand. War was days away.

chapters.title: War and Genocide
chapters.text:
On the first of September 1939, Germany invaded Poland. Two days later, Britain and France declared war. Poland was crushed within weeks, and the Soviet Union occupied its eastern half, as agreed in the secret pact. From the start, this was a war of a different kind. Behind the army came SS units that murdered Polish intellectuals, priests and Jews. The Nazis planned to turn Eastern Europe into living space for Germans, and its peoples into a population of slaves.

In the spring of 1940, Germany struck in the west. Denmark and Norway fell, then the Netherlands, Belgium and, in just six weeks, France. Hitler was at the height of his power. Only Britain, under Winston Churchill, kept fighting, and in the Battle of Britain the German air force failed to win control of the skies.

On the twenty-second of June 1941, Hitler launched his real war: the invasion of the Soviet Union, with more than three million soldiers. It was conceived from the start as a war of annihilation. Millions of Soviet prisoners of war were deliberately starved to death. Behind the front, mobile killing squads, the Einsatzgruppen, supported by police battalions and regular army units, shot Jewish men, women and children by the hundreds of thousands. At Babi Yar, near Kyiv, more than thirty-three thousand Jews were murdered in two days. The German advance reached the outskirts of Moscow but was stopped in December by the Soviet counterattack and the Russian winter. That same month, after Japan attacked Pearl Harbor, Hitler declared war on the United States.

The murder of the Jews of Europe now became systematic. In January 1942, at a villa on the Wannsee lake in Berlin, senior officials met to coordinate what they called the final solution of the Jewish question. Extermination camps were built in occupied Poland: Belzec, Sobibor, Treblinka, Chelmno, Majdanek, and the largest of all, Auschwitz-Birkenau. Jews were deported there by train from every corner of occupied Europe, from France and the Netherlands to Greece and Hungary, and murdered in gas chambers, most within hours of arrival. About six million Jews were killed in the Holocaust. The Nazis also murdered hundreds of thousands of Roma and Sinti, disabled people, and countless others they deemed enemies or inferior.

The turning point of the war came in the winter of 1942 to 1943, at Stalingrad, where an entire German army was surrounded and destroyed. In North Africa, German and Italian forces were defeated. From then on, the Red Army pushed relentlessly west. In June 1944, the Western Allies landed in Normandy. Germany's cities were being reduced to rubble by British and American bombers. Hamburg, Cologne, Dresden and Berlin were devastated, and hundreds of thousands of civilians were killed.

There was resistance in Germany, but it was small and isolated: communists and socialists, church figures, the students of the White Rose in Munich, and individuals who hid Jews. In July 1944, a group of army officers tried to kill Hitler with a bomb at his headquarters in East Prussia. Colonel Claus von Stauffenberg planted the bomb, but Hitler survived. Stauffenberg was shot that night in the courtyard of the army headquarters in Berlin, and thousands of suspects were arrested.

The last months of the war were the bloodiest. In January 1945, millions of Germans fled west before the advancing Red Army. In April, Soviet forces launched their final offensive across the Oder and encircled Berlin. Old men and teenage boys were sent to fight in the streets. In his bunker under the Reich Chancellery, Hitler killed himself on the thirtieth of April. Berlin surrendered on the second of May, and Germany capitulated unconditionally on the eighth of May 1945.

The war in Europe had killed more than thirty-five million people, among them some twenty-five million citizens of the Soviet Union. Germany lay in ruins. Germans would later call this moment Stunde Null, zero hour. Everything would have to begin again.

chapters.title: Division and Reunification
chapters.text:
In the summer of 1945, the victorious powers met at Potsdam, just outside Berlin. Germany lost its eastern territories to Poland and the Soviet Union, and around twelve million Germans were expelled or fled from Eastern Europe. What remained was divided into four zones of occupation: American, British, French and Soviet. Berlin, deep inside the Soviet zone, was divided into four sectors too. The women of Berlin, the Trümmerfrauen, began clearing the rubble by hand. At Nuremberg, the surviving Nazi leaders were put on trial.

The wartime alliance soon fell apart. The Soviets built a communist system in their zone, while the Western powers merged theirs and introduced a new currency, the Deutsche Mark. In June 1948, Stalin responded by blocking all land access to West Berlin. The Americans and British answered with the Berlin Airlift: for almost a year, planes landed every few minutes at Tempelhof and other airfields, supplying two million people with food and coal. Stalin gave up. The former enemy had become a partner.

In 1949, two German states were founded. In the west, the Federal Republic of Germany, with its capital in Bonn and Konrad Adenauer as chancellor, a parliamentary democracy anchored in the West and, from 1955, in NATO. In the east, the German Democratic Republic, the GDR, a one-party state under the Socialist Unity Party, closely controlled by Moscow. West Germany experienced an economic miracle, the Wirtschaftswunder. East Germany struggled. On the seventeenth of June 1953, workers rose up across the GDR, beginning on the Stalinallee in Berlin. Soviet tanks crushed the uprising.

The weak point was Berlin. Between East and West Berlin the border was still open, and East Germans could simply take the underground to the West. By 1961, around two and a half million people had fled, many of them young and skilled. On the night of the thirteenth of August 1961, East German soldiers and police sealed the border with barbed wire. Within days, they began building a wall. Families were separated overnight. Over the following years it grew into a deadly system of concrete walls, watchtowers, dogs and a death strip. At least a hundred and forty people were killed at the Berlin Wall trying to escape.

Berlin became the front line of the Cold War. In 1963, President Kennedy came to West Berlin and declared, Ich bin ein Berliner. In the GDR, the Stasi, the secret police, built one of the most extensive surveillance systems in history, with tens of thousands of officers and many more informers. In West Germany, a younger generation began to ask their parents what they had done under the Nazis, and the student movement of 1968 forced a reckoning with the past. In 1970, Chancellor Willy Brandt knelt at the memorial to the Warsaw Ghetto, and his Ostpolitik brought a cautious détente with the East.

In the 1980s, the Soviet Union, under Mikhail Gorbachev, began to reform. The GDR's ageing leader, Erich Honecker, refused to follow. In the summer of 1989, Hungary opened its border with Austria, and thousands of East Germans fled through it. In the autumn, mass protests spread across the GDR, above all in Leipzig, where every Monday tens of thousands marched with candles, chanting: We are the people. The protests stayed peaceful, and this time no tanks came. Honecker was forced out.

On the evening of the ninth of November 1989, a government spokesman, Günter Schabowski, announced at a press conference new rules allowing East Germans to travel. Asked when they would take effect, he looked at his notes and said: immediately, without delay. Thousands of East Berliners rushed to the border crossings. At Bornholmer Strasse, the overwhelmed guards finally opened the gate. That night, people danced on the Wall at the Brandenburg Gate. The ninth of November, the date of the republic in 1918 and of the pogrom in 1938, now became the date of freedom.

Eleven months later, on the third of October 1990, Germany was reunified. Berlin became its capital again, and the Reichstag, with its new glass dome, once more the home of a democratic parliament. As you walk through the city, you will see all these layers, often side by side: the Prussian monuments, the scars of war, the traces of the Wall, and the memorials with which Germany has chosen to remember, rather than forget, its past. Enjoy your journey.
